reviews.scopeMarkdown: Bài gốc: **182 từ**, đếm bằng cách tách nguyên văn theo khoảng trắng; nằm trong yêu cầu 150–200 từ. Cô chỉ chấm bài Đề 1 đã gõ, không chấm Đề 2 hoặc bản scan.
reviews.overall: Em cần sửa và nộp lại. Câu mở Detail 1 dùng “total citizents” khiến tỷ lệ phần trăm nữ nghị sĩ thành tỷ lệ trong toàn dân; “was” cũng chưa hòa hợp với nhóm người em nêu. Em còn gọi mức tăng từ 25% lên 37% là “slightly” và đặt “Despite this significant increase” trước nhận xét về năm 2000. Overview thiếu thông tin thấp nhất. Em đã dùng được cấu trúc with và after which, nhưng phải gắn chúng với đúng dữ liệu. Cô yêu cầu em đọc lại kiến thức đã ghi chép và tự sửa các câu được đánh dấu.
reviews.dataGrouping: Detail 1 trình bày France trước, rồi Germany và Italy; Detail 2 trình bày UK rồi Belgium. Nhóm đầu có tỷ lệ phần trăm cao hơn ở cuối kỳ, còn hai nước trong nhóm sau cùng đạt khoảng 28% năm 2012, nên Cô giữ nhóm và thứ tự của em. Em đã chọn đỉnh năm 2004 của France; phần cần bổ sung là các mốc đầu–cuối của Germany và Italy để việc so sánh rõ hơn.

reviews.originalEssay:
The given line chart illustrates the percentage of female parliamentarians in five European countries over a 12-year period, commencing in 2000.
Overall, there was a general increase in the share of women serving in parliament in most of the studied nations, with the UK witnessing the most pronounced rise. Also of note is that Italy had the highest figure at the end of the period.
 To elaborate, in 2000, 25% of the total citizents in France was female representatives, went up slightly to 37% in 2004 before decreasing to 31% in 2012. The figures for Germany and Italy, conversely, grew by roughly 4% and 13% respectively over the entire period.
Regarding the remaining categories, the most noticeable upturn was seen in the UK, rising from around 3% in 2000 to 28% after 12 years. Despite this significant increase, the proportion of women in parliament in this country still remained the lowest in 2000. Similarly, in 2000, the figure for Belgium started at 17%, after which it rose gradually to 28% in 2004 and finally remained relatively stable at around 28–29% until 2012.

reviews.originalEssay:
The given pie charts illustrate the main reasons why students chose a particular university in the UK in 1997 and 2007.
Overall, there was an increase in the proportions of students choosing suitable degree courses, proximity to parental home and quality of teaching, while an opposite trend was observed in quality of resources and good sports and social activities. Also of note is that suitable degree courses consistently had the highest figures throughout the years
To elaborate, in 1997, 10% of students chose a university because of its proximity to their parental home, and this figure rose progressively to 22% in 2007. The figures for suitable degree courses and quality of teaching; likewise, increased by 2% and 3% respectively over the entire period.
Regarding the remaining categories, the proportion of students choosing a university because of the quality of its resources declined slightly from 21% to 17% between 1997 and 2007. The figure for good sports and social activities also decreased, but to a far greater extent, falling by 13% over the same period.

reviews.originalEssay:
The pie charts illustrate the proportions of people migrating to and from the UK for different reasons in 2007.
Overall, it is clear that having a definite job was the most common reason for both immigration and emigration. Also of note is that formal study was considerably more significant among immigrants, while the opposite trend was true in the case of emigrants.
To elaborate, an impressive 30% and 29% of people migrating to and from the UK, respectively, were recorded as moving for a definite job. The proportion of people migrating to the UK for formal study stood at 26%, considerably higher than the figure for those leaving the country, at just 4%. In contrast, looking for work accounted for 12% of immigration, compared with a significantly higher 22% of emigration.
As for accompanying or joining someone, the percentages were relatively similar, at 15% for immigration and 13% for emigration. Meanwhile, the figure for those who did not state a reason was three times as high among emigrants as among immigrants, at 18% and 6%, respectively.
